claim: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) provides a major source of genetic variation.
source: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) provides a major source of genetic variation.
evidence: This is a general statement about HGT that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Many viruses, including poxviruses, encode genes with crucial functions directly gained by gene transfer from hosts.
source: Many viruses, including poxviruses, encode genes with crucial functions directly gained by gene transfer from hosts.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and is referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: The mechanism of transfer to poxvirus genomes is unknown.
source: The mechanism of transfer to poxvirus genomes is unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses, based on the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: Long Interspersed Nuclear Element-1 retrotransposition plays a central role in HGT to virus genomes.
source: Using genome analysis and experimental screens of infected cells, we discovered a central role for Long Interspersed Nuclear Element-1 retrotransposition in HGT to virus genomes.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by both genome analysis and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The process of LINE-1 mediated HGT to poxvirus genomes recapitulates processed pseudogene generation, but with host messenger RNA directed into virus genomes.
source: The process recapitulates processed pseudogene generation, but with host messenger RNA directed into virus genomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and comparison with known LINE-1 mechanisms in host genomes.

claim: Hallmark features of retrotransposition favor virus adaptation through rapid duplication of captured host genes on arrival.
source: Intriguingly, hallmark features of retrotransposition appear to favor virus adaption through rapid duplication of captured host genes on arrival.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of gene duplications in recovered isolates.

claim: HGT bypasses vertical inheritance from parent to offspring.
source: The movement of genetic material from one organism to another by horizontal gene transfer (HGT) bypasses vertical inheritance from parent to offspring (Keeling and Palmer, 2008).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HGT can shortcut more gradual mutational processes by providing the opportunity for adaptive leaps through single mutational events where genes can be transferred between genomes across kingdoms of life.
source: HGT can shortcut more gradual mutational processes by providing the opportunity for adaptive leaps through single mutational events where genes can be transferred between genomes across kingdoms of life (Keeling and Palmer, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HGT plays a central role in the diversification of many infectious microbes.
source: HGT plays a central role in the diversification of many infectious microbes, which contend with complex environments and host immune defenses to persist and replicate.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: HGT is particularly well-described in bacteria, where it can contribute to the emerging crisis of multi-antibiotic resistant pathogens.
source: HGT is particularly well-described in bacteria, where it can contribute to the emerging crisis of multi-antibiotic resistant pathogens (Wijayawardena et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Many classes of viruses acquire genes from the hosts they infect by horizontal transfer.
source: Many classes of viruses acquire genes from the hosts they infect by horizontal transfer (Caprari et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Recognition of the horizontal transfer of the host c-Src gene into the Rous Sarcoma virus genome led to the discovery of oncogenes.
source: A conspicuous example is Rous Sarcoma virus, in which recognition of the horizontal transfer of the host c-Src gene into the virus genome led to the discovery of oncogenes (Swanstrom et al., 1983).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Other co-opted host genes diverge to aid the virus in inhibiting host defenses.
source: Other co-opted host genes diverge to aid the virus in inhibiting host defenses (Kawagishi-Kobayashi et al., 1997; Elde and Malik, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The acquisition of host genes is a common mechanism by which viruses of many classes gain adaptive advantages to propagate.
source: It has become increasingly clear that the acquisition of host genes is a common mechanism by which viruses of many classes gain adaptive advantages to propagate (Dolja and Koonin, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The mechanisms by which genes are transferred from host to virus genomes are not well understood.
source: Despite the prevalence of HGT in diverse viruses and its importance in virus evolution, the mechanisms by which genes are transferred from host to virus genomes are not well understood.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap based on the state of the field.

claim: More than 25% of poxvirus genes were acquired by HGT from hosts based on phylogenetic analysis.
source: Based on phylogenetic analysis, more than 25% of poxvirus genes were acquired by HGT from hosts (Hughes and Friedman, 2005), although similarities not evident in sequence comparisons but revealed by shared protein structures suggest that a higher proportion of genes were acquired by horizontal transfer (Bahar et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Similarities revealed by shared protein structures suggest that a higher proportion of poxvirus genes than 25% were acquired by horizontal transfer.
source: Based on phylogenetic analysis, more than 25% of poxvirus genes were acquired by HGT from hosts (Hughes and Friedman, 2005), although similarities not evident in sequence comparisons but revealed by shared protein structures suggest that a higher proportion of genes were acquired by horizontal transfer (Bahar et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Many captured poxvirus genes adapt to act as inhibitors of host immune defenses to favor virus replication.
source: Many captured genes adapt to act as inhibitors of host immune defenses to favor virus replication (Elde and Malik, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Some captured poxvirus genes act as host range factors because their deletion leads to restriction of infectible cell types or species.
source: Some act as host range factors because their deletion leads to restriction of infectible cell types or species, implying that new acquisitions may aid in host jumps (Bratke et al., 2013; Haller et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: New acquisitions of host genes by poxviruses may aid in host jumps.
source: Some act as host range factors because their deletion leads to restriction of infectible cell types or species, implying that new acquisitions may aid in host jumps (Bratke et al., 2013; Haller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some genes act as host range factors, supported by citations.

claim: Variola virus, which caused smallpox, has been eradicated.
source: While the most notorious poxvirus, variola virus which caused smallpox, has been eradicated, other extant poxviruses are capable of infecting humans and pose the risk of new pandemics, as appears to be the case for monkeypox (Sklenovská and Van Ranst, 2018).
evidence: This is a well-established historical fact supported by citation.

claim: Other extant poxviruses are capable of infecting humans and pose the risk of new pandemics.
source: While the most notorious poxvirus, variola virus which caused smallpox, has been eradicated, other extant poxviruses are capable of infecting humans and pose the risk of new pandemics, as appears to be the case for monkeypox (Sklenovská and Van Ranst, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Poxviruses serve as useful model systems for other viruses with large double-stranded (ds) DNA genomes.
source: Poxviruses also serve as useful model systems for other viruses with large double-stranded (ds) DNA genomes (Deeg et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Poxvirus-encoded copies of host genes lack introns.
source: Because poxvirus-encoded copies of host genes lack introns, it was hypothesized that transfer occurs through a spliced mRNA intermediate (Lefkowitz et al., 2006).
evidence: This observation is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It was hypothesized that transfer of host genes to poxviruses occurs through a spliced mRNA intermediate.
source: Because poxvirus-encoded copies of host genes lack introns, it was hypothesized that transfer occurs through a spliced mRNA intermediate (Lefkowitz et al., 2006).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: For integration, mRNA templates need to be reverse transcribed into virus genomes by either a retrovirus or a retrotransposon.
source: For integration, mRNA templates need to be reverse transcribed into virus genomes by either a retrovirus or a retrotransposon.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of molecular mechanisms.

claim: A provirus is encoded in the genome of fowlpox virus.
source: The discovery of a provirus encoded in the genome of fowlpox virus (Hertig et al., 1997) and a Short Interspersed Nuclear Element (SINE) retrotransposon found in the taterapox virus genome (Piskurek and Okada, 2007) indicate that either is capable of catalyzing insertions in poxvirus genomes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A Short Interspersed Nuclear Element (SINE) retrotransposon is found in the taterapox virus genome.
source: The discovery of a provirus encoded in the genome of fowlpox virus (Hertig et al., 1997) and a Short Interspersed Nuclear Element (SINE) retrotransposon found in the taterapox virus genome (Piskurek and Okada, 2007) indicate that either is capable of catalyzing insertions in poxvirus genomes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Either retroviruses or retrotransposons are capable of catalyzing insertions in poxvirus genomes.
source: The discovery of a provirus encoded in the genome of fowlpox virus (Hertig et al., 1997) and a Short Interspersed Nuclear Element (SINE) retrotransposon found in the taterapox virus genome (Piskurek and Okada, 2007) indicate that either is capable of catalyzing insertions in poxvirus genomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited discoveries of provirus and SINE elements in poxvirus genomes.

claim: LINE-1 retrotransposons reverse transcribe and integrate host genes in a sequence independent manner, resulting in collections of processed pseudogenes in diverse host genomes.
source: Long Interspersed Nuclear Element-1 (LINE-1) retrotransposons are known to reverse transcribe and integrate host genes in a sequence independent manner, resulting in collections of processed pseudogenes in diverse host genomes (Esnault et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LINE-1 transcripts encode two proteins: an RNA binding protein (ORF1) and an endonuclease (EN)/reverse transcriptase (RT) protein (ORF2).
source: LINE-1 transcripts encode two proteins: an RNA binding protein (ORF1) and an endonuclease (EN)/reverse transcriptase (RT) protein (ORF2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about LINE-1 structure.

claim: ORF2 preferentially nicks one strand of DNA at a TTTT/AA site in the host genome.
source: ORF2 preferentially nicks one strand of DNA at a TTTT/AA site in the host genome, and reverse transcription is primed from the exposed 3′hydroxl.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LINE-1 mechanism.

claim: Reverse transcription is primed from the exposed 3′hydroxyl after ORF2 nicks DNA.
source: ORF2 preferentially nicks one strand of DNA at a TTTT/AA site in the host genome, and reverse transcription is primed from the exposed 3′hydroxl.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LINE-1 mechanism.

claim: LINE-1 elements can integrate at sites of dsDNA breaks in an endonuclease-independent manner.
source: LINE-1 elements can also integrate at sites of dsDNA breaks in an endonuclease-independent manner (Morrish et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LINE-1 RT shows cis-preference, meaning it is most likely to transcribe the RNA from which it was translated.
source: LINE-1 RT shows cis-preference, meaning it is most likely to transcribe the RNA from which it was translated, but SINE elements like the one found in the taterapox genome can hijack LINE-1 machinery to integrate following replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LINE-1 mechanism.

claim: SINE elements can hijack LINE-1 machinery to integrate following replication.
source: LINE-1 RT shows cis-preference, meaning it is most likely to transcribe the RNA from which it was translated, but SINE elements like the one found in the taterapox genome can hijack LINE-1 machinery to integrate following replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SINE and LINE-1 interaction.

claim: LINE-1 enzymes promiscuously reverse transcribe host mRNA, which might facilitate transfers of host genes to virus genomes.
source: Sometimes LINE-1 enzymes promiscuously reverse transcribe host mRNA, which might facilitate transfers of host genes to virus genomes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on known LINE-1 behavior.

claim: The poly(A) tail of host mRNA or a poly(A) tract in SINE transcripts may initialize LINE-1 reverse transcription.
source: It is plausible that the poly(A) tail of either the host mRNA or a poly(A) tract in SINE transcripts initializes LINE-1 reverse transcription, in addition to faithful recognition of LINE-1 transcripts.
evidence: This is a plausible mechanism based on known LINE-1 behavior.

claim: Short target site duplications (TSDs) of sequences ~8–20 bp flank LINE-1 insertions.
source: Short target site duplications (TSDs) of sequences ~8–20 bp flank LINE-1 insertions of either LINE-1 or host sequences, likely a product of repairing staggered breaks during integration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LINE-1 insertions.

claim: TSDs flanking LINE-1 insertions are likely a product of repairing staggered breaks during integration.
source: Short target site duplications (TSDs) of sequences ~8–20 bp flank LINE-1 insertions of either LINE-1 or host sequences, likely a product of repairing staggered breaks during integration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of TSD formation.

claim: LINE-1-mediated flanking duplications are copies of host sequences as opposed to specific retrovirus sequences.
source: The resulting LINE-1-mediated flanking duplications are copies of host sequences as opposed to specific retrovirus sequences.
evidence: This distinguishes LINE-1 from retroviral mechanisms based on established knowledge.

claim: Viruses rapidly mutate, and unique signatures of retrovirus or LINE-1-mediated horizontal transfer may quickly degrade and obscure mechanisms of transfer.
source: However, given that viruses rapidly mutate, unique signatures of retrovirus or LINE-1-mediated horizontal transfer may quickly degrade and obscure mechanisms of transfer.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of viral mutation rates and inference about signature degradation.

claim: Virus homologs of the host Golgi Anti-Apoptotic Protein (GAAP) found in several orthopoxviruses are ~75% identical to human GAAP.
source: Virus homologs of the host Golgi Anti-Apoptotic Protein (GAAP; also called transmembrane Bax inhibitor motif protein family 4 or TMBIM4), found in several orthopoxviruses, are ~75% identical to human GAAP (Gubser et al., 2007; Saraiva et al., 2013), suggesting a recent acquisition and/or highly conserved function favoring virus replication.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The high identity between virus and human GAAP suggests a recent acquisition and/or highly conserved function favoring virus replication.
source: Virus homologs of the host Golgi Anti-Apoptotic Protein (GAAP; also called transmembrane Bax inhibitor motif protein family 4 or TMBIM4), found in several orthopoxviruses, are ~75% identical to human GAAP (Gubser et al., 2007; Saraiva et al., 2013), suggesting a recent acquisition and/or highly conserved function favoring virus replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the high sequence identity observed.

claim: Nearly identical 21 base pair sequences flank the open reading frame of virus GAAP (vGAAP), indicative of a TSD.
source: Strikingly, we observed nearly identical 21 base pair sequences flanking the open reading frame of virus GAAP (vGAAP), indicative of a TSD, consistent with gene capture resulting from LINE-1-mediated retrotransposition of host mRNA (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The flanking sequences of vGAAP are consistent with gene capture resulting from LINE-1-mediated retrotransposition of host mRNA.
source: Strikingly, we observed nearly identical 21 base pair sequences flanking the open reading frame of virus GAAP (vGAAP), indicative of a TSD, consistent with gene capture resulting from LINE-1-mediated retrotransposition of host mRNA (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed TSD pattern.

claim: The vGAAP gene is situated near one of two identical inverted terminal repeat (ITR) regions of the virus genome.
source: The vGAAP gene is situated near one of two identical inverted terminal repeat (ITR) regions of the virus genome, and on opposite ends of the genome in various viruses, suggesting that it was originally transferred into the ITR.
evidence: This is an observation from genome analysis.

claim: vGAAP is on opposite ends of the genome in various viruses, suggesting that it was originally transferred into the ITR.
source: The vGAAP gene is situated near one of two identical inverted terminal repeat (ITR) regions of the virus genome, and on opposite ends of the genome in various viruses, suggesting that it was originally transferred into the ITR.
evidence: This is inferred from the genomic location patterns observed.

claim: A single copy of the putative 21 bp TSD at an analogous position near the other ITR in the cowpox genome suggests a pseudo-empty site.
source: A single copy of the putative 21 bp TSD at an analogous position near the other ITR in the cowpox genome suggests a pseudo-empty site (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the genomic data shown in the figure.

claim: Host genes can be retrotransposed into poxvirus genomes by LINE-1 activity in a process akin to the generation of processed pseudogenes.
source: Taken together, with a published account of a non-autonomous SINE in the genome of taterapox virus (Piskurek and Okada, 2007), these observations suggest that host genes can be retrotransposed into poxvirus genomes by LINE-1 activity in a process akin to the generation of processed pseudogenes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations of vGAAP and the cited SINE element.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis revealed a single origin for the horizontal transfer of GAAP into poxvirus genomes.
source: Phylogenetic analysis revealed a single origin for the horizontal transfer of GAAP into poxvirus genomes.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: At least two other classes of DNA viruses, herpesviruses and iridoviruses, independently acquired GAAP by horizontal transfer.
source: In addition, at least two other classes of DNA viruses, herpesviruses and iridoviruses, independently acquired GAAP by horizontal transfer (Figure 1B; Bellehumeur et al., 2016; de Groof et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations.

claim: The S1 gene of Squirrel Monkey cytomegalovirus encodes a protein more than 95% identical to squirrel monkey SLAMF6, followed by portions of the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the host mRNA.
source: Another study of Squirrel Monkey cytomegalovirus revealed that the S1 gene encodes a protein more than 95% identical to squirrel monkey Signaling lymphocytic activation molecule family 6 (SLAMF6), followed by portions of the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the host mRNA (Pérez-Carmona et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Many DNA viruses acquire host genes by retrotransposition.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that many DNA viruses acquire host genes by retrotransposition.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple examples of HGT with retrotransposition signatures.

claim: The majority of host to virus gene transfers lack signatures of retrotransposition, which can quickly degrade through mutation.
source: However, the majority of host to virus gene transfers lack signatures of retrotransposition, which can quickly degrade through mutation, motivating our development of an experimental strategy for capturing HGT events in real time.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that few transfers show clear signatures.

claim: Vaccinia virus (Copenhagen strain) encodes nearly 200 genes in a 191,737 bp genome.
source: We developed a selection scheme using vaccinia virus (Copenhagen strain), which encodes nearly 200 genes in a 191,737 bp genome (See Materials and methods).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the vaccinia virus genome.

claim: K3L was presumably acquired from a host by an ancient poxvirus based on sequence identity with human eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (eIF2α; 27.6% identical).
source: We focused on K3L, a gene that was presumably acquired from a host by an ancient poxvirus based on sequence identity with human eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (eIF2α; 27.6% identical) (Beattie et al., 1991; Elde et al., 2009; Elde and Malik, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: K3L diverged from eIF2α to encode a protein that blocks the host defense Protein Kinase R (PKR) pathway.
source: K3L diverged from eIF2α to encode a protein that blocks the host defense Protein Kinase R (PKR) pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about K3L function.

claim: PKR is activated by dsRNA produced by viruses in the cytoplasm during transcription of virus genes and virus replication.
source: PKR is activated by dsRNA produced by viruses in the cytoplasm during transcription of virus genes and virus replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKR activation.

claim: Upon activation, PKR phosphorylates eIF2α, leading to a block in protein translation and virus replication.
source: Upon activation, PKR phosphorylates eIF2α, leading to a block in protein translation and virus replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKR function.

claim: K3L acts as a pseudo-substrate of PKR to competitively inhibit PKR from binding eIF2α.
source: K3L acts as a pseudo-substrate of PKR to competitively inhibit PKR from binding eIF2α (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Beattie et al., 1991; Kawagishi-Kobayashi et al., 1997), and can be essential for productive infections depending on the host (Langland and Jacobs, 2002; Park et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in a figure.

claim: K3L can be essential for productive infections depending on the host.
source: K3L acts as a pseudo-substrate of PKR to competitively inhibit PKR from binding eIF2α (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Beattie et al., 1991; Kawagishi-Kobayashi et al., 1997), and can be essential for productive infections depending on the host (Langland and Jacobs, 2002; Park et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Viruses lacking K3L replicate poorly in BHK cells.
source: Viruses lacking K3L replicate poorly in BHK cells, providing strong selection for viruses that 'reclaimed' the mCherry-K3L gene by horizontal transfer and/or somehow adapted in the absence of K3L to block host PKR and regain productive replication.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Ten virus isolates were recovered from mCherry-positive infected cell clones after screening ~500 million viruses.
source: Using this scheme, we screened ~500 million viruses over many experiments and recovered ten virus isolates from mCherry-positive infected cell clones.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results.

claim: Viruses encoding K3L replicate ~100-fold better than the parent virus deleted for K3L in the restrictive BHK cells.
source: In the restrictive BHK cells, viruses encoding K3L replicate ~100-fold better than the parent virus deleted for K3L (Figure 2B), allowing us to identify viruses with improved replication compared to the larger population of K3L-deficient viruses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Each recovered virus isolate infected BHK cells with titers on par with viruses encoding K3L.
source: After plaque purification of candidate mCherry positive isolates, we infected BHK cells with each recovered virus isolate and observed titers on par with viruses encoding K3L (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mCherry-K3L fusion gene was integrated into the virus genome at a unique position in every isolate.
source: By sequencing the genome of each recovered virus isolate, we found that the mCherry-K3L fusion gene was integrated into the virus genome at a unique position in every isolate (Figures 2D and 3A), providing the opportunity to compare each independent integration event.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in the figures.

claim: All integrations were consistent with a mechanism of LINE-1 retrotransposition-mediated HGT.
source: All integrations were consistent with a mechanism of LINE-1 retrotransposition-mediated HGT.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of all recovered isolates.

claim: The sequence of each transferred gene revealed hallmark features of mRNA gene capture, including 5′ and 3′ UTRs, precise intron splicing, and poly(A) tails.
source: The sequence of each transferred gene revealed hallmark features of mRNA gene capture, including 5′ and 3′ UTRs, precise intron splicing, and poly(A) tails (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For 7 of 10 isolates, TSDs flanked mCherry-K3L insertions and contained cut site sequences matching the consensus (TTTT/AA) of LINE-1 endonuclease.
source: For 7 of 10 isolates, TSDs flanked mCherry-K3L insertions and contained cut site sequences matching the consensus (TTTT/AA) of LINE-1 endonuclease (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in the figures.

claim: Integrations in isolates 5, 9, and 10 lacking TSDs might result from an endonuclease-independent LINE-1 mechanism at DNA breaks.
source: Although there were no TSDs flanking mCherry-K3L in isolates 5, 9, and 10, these integrations might result from an endonuclease-independent LINE-1 mechanism at DNA breaks (Morrish et al., 2002).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of TSDs and supported by citation to prior work on endonuclease-independent mechanisms.

claim: Robust LINE-1 activity was detected in RK13 cells.
source: Because our experiments lack any exogenous reverse transcriptase, we tested for endogenous activity in the RK13 cells and detected robust LINE-1 activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: LINE-1-mediated retrotransposition may be a common mechanism of HGT in poxvirus genomes.
source: These results suggest that LINE-1-mediated retrotransposition may be a common mechanism of HGT in poxvirus genomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing LINE-1 signatures in all recovered isolates.

claim: LINE-1-mediated retrotransposition may be more likely than retroviral mechanisms simply because LINE-1 enzymes are nearly ubiquitous in mammals.
source: While we do not exclude the possibility that genes can also be transposed into the viral genome by retroviruses, this would require co-infection. LINE-1-mediated retrotransposition may be more likely simply because LINE-1 enzymes are nearly ubiquitous in mammals.
evidence: This is inferred from the ubiquity of LINE-1 elements and the requirement for co-infection in retroviral mechanisms.

claim: Poxvirus genomes are arranged with essential genes shared by all poxviruses in the central region of the genome.
source: In general, poxvirus genomes are arranged with the essential genes, shared by all poxviruses, in the central region of the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about poxvirus genome organization.

claim: Clade- or species-specific genes, which more commonly exhibit evidence of HGT, are enriched near the ends of the poxvirus genome.
source: Clade- or species-specific genes, which more commonly exhibit evidence of HGT, are enriched near the ends of the genome (Lefkowitz et al., 2006; McLysaght et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pattern of gene distribution may reflect that gene transfer into the central genomic region is more likely to interrupt genes vital for virus replication.
source: This pattern may reflect that gene transfer into the central genomic region genome is more likely to interrupt genes vital for virus replication (Lefkowitz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed pattern and supported by citation.

claim: All but 1 of the 10 isolates integrated K3L outside a roughly defined central region of the genome containing 90 core chordopoxvirus genes.
source: Consistent with this, all but 1 of the 10 isolates, we recovered integrated K3L outside a roughly defined central region of the genome containing 90 core chordopoxvirus genes (Lefkowitz et al., 2006; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citation.

claim: In isolate 5, the K3L integration involved a duplication of two essential genes, G9R and L1R.
source: In the case of isolate 5, the K3L integration involved a duplication of two essential genes, G9R and L1R (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In a contemporaneous study, virus genomes that acquired a host gene by horizontal transfer within a duplicated gene also propagated.
source: In a contemporaneous study (Rahman et al., 2022), virus genomes that acquired a host gene by horizontal transfer within a duplicated gene also propagated.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to another study.

claim: In both cases of gene duplication, gene functions were preserved by duplication.
source: In both cases, gene functions were preserved by duplication.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that viruses with duplicated genes remained viable.

claim: Spurious gene duplications can appear frequently in poxvirus genomes.
source: Spurious gene duplications can appear frequently in poxvirus genomes (Hughes and Friedman, 2005), pointing to a flexible means of poxvirus adaptation involving horizontal transfer even into essential genes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Gene duplications point to a flexible means of poxvirus adaptation involving horizontal transfer even into essential genes.
source: Spurious gene duplications can appear frequently in poxvirus genomes (Hughes and Friedman, 2005), pointing to a flexible means of poxvirus adaptation involving horizontal transfer even into essential genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of gene duplications and their role in maintaining viability.

claim: Duplication of poxvirus genes, followed by rapid gene copy amplification, can boost virus replication.
source: Previous studies found that duplication of poxvirus genes, followed by rapid gene copy amplification, can boost virus replication (Brennan et al., 2014; Elde et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Two isolates (4 and 5) showed polymorphic copy number increases of K3L.
source: In our analysis, we discovered two isolates where K3L had undergone polymorphic copy number increases (isolates 4 and 5; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Homologous recombination in poxviruses requires as little as 16 bp of homology.
source: Homologous recombination, including unequal crossovers leading to duplications, requires as little as 16 bp of homology in poxviruses (Yao and Evans, 2001), suggesting that LINE-1 induced TSDs might facilitate gene amplification.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LINE-1 induced TSDs might facilitate gene amplification.
source: Homologous recombination, including unequal crossovers leading to duplications, requires as little as 16 bp of homology in poxviruses (Yao and Evans, 2001), suggesting that LINE-1 induced TSDs might facilitate gene amplification.
evidence: This is inferred from the minimal homology requirement and the presence of TSDs.

claim: Genes transferred within the ITR are duplicated on the other end by replication-based mechanisms.
source: Genes transferred within the ITR are duplicated on the other end by replication-based mechanisms (McFadden and Dales, 1979), as we observed in isolates 4 and 9 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation and experimental observations.

claim: Genes integrated near the termini of the genome by HGT may be especially prone to duplication due to stretches of short, high copy tandem repeats found in and near the ITR regions.
source: Genes integrated near the termini of the genome by HGT, like isolate 4, may be especially prone to duplication due to stretches of short, high copy tandem repeats found in and near the ITR regions (Figure 4A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the genomic features and observed duplications.

claim: HGT occurs evenly across poxvirus genomes, but with an enrichment of transferred genes persisting near the ends, where insults to essential genes are less probable and duplication-based adaptation is favored.
source: These observations are consistent with the idea that HGT occurs evenly across poxvirus genomes, but with an enrichment of transferred genes persisting near the ends, where insults to essential genes are less probable and duplication-based adaptation is favored (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and genomic patterns.

claim: Gene families found only in specific lineages of poxviruses are more likely to be present in multiple copies than single-copy host-acquired genes found among diverse poxviruses.
source: Along these lines, gene families found only in specific lineages of poxviruses, indicating more recent acquisition, are more likely to be present in multiple copies than single-copy host-acquired genes found among diverse poxviruses (Hughes and Friedman, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Recombinant viruses encoding eIF2α in place of K3L replicate weakly.
source: We performed four serial infections of viruses expressing eIF2α or an eIF2α variant lacking the PKR phosphorylation site (S51A) in RK13 cells. While the recombinant viruses replicate weakly, we observed a nearly tenfold increase in virus replication for both eIF2α-encoding viruses after passaging (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A nearly tenfold increase in virus replication was observed for both eIF2α-encoding viruses after passaging.
source: We performed four serial infections of viruses expressing eIF2α or an eIF2α variant lacking the PKR phosphorylation site (S51A) in RK13 cells. While the recombinant viruses replicate weakly, we observed a nearly tenfold increase in virus replication for both eIF2α-encoding viruses after passaging (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Independent gene copy increases of eIF2α were found in both evolved virus isolates.
source: By sequencing the eIF2α region in evolved virus isolates, we found independent gene copy increases of eIF2α in both viruses (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Gene copy increases following HGT play a critical role in poxvirus evolution.
source: These results support a critical role for gene copy increases following HGT in poxvirus evolution, as also observed for K3L and other genes (Brennan et al., 2014; Elde et al., 2012) and suggest a common pathway facilitating adaptation of host genes captured by poxviruses.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is a common pathway facilitating adaptation of host genes captured by poxviruses.
source: These results support a critical role for gene copy increases following HGT in poxvirus evolution, as also observed for K3L and other genes (Brennan et al., 2014; Elde et al., 2012) and suggest a common pathway facilitating adaptation of host genes captured by poxviruses.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistent observation of gene copy increases across different experiments.

claim: HGT is an important process facilitating virus evolution.
source: HGT is an important process facilitating virus evolution (Caprari et al., 2015; Deeg et al., 2018; Hughes and Friedman, 2005; Koonin and Yutin, 2019; McLysaght et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Retrotransposition to virus genomes could greatly extend the range of LINE-1 or related elements that subsequently mobilize to a newly infected virus host.
source: In addition to self-propagation in host genomes, retrotransposition to virus genomes could greatly extend the range of LINE-1 or related elements that subsequently mobilize to a newly infected virus host (Piskurek and Okada, 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: The extensive host range of some poxviruses suggests the possibility of cross-host lineage transfer of LINE-1s, non-autonomous SINEs, and host transcripts between mammals.
source: The extensive host range of some poxviruses, for example, between rodent and primate species, suggests the possibility of cross-host lineage transfer of LINE-1s, non-autonomous SINEs, and host transcripts between mammals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known host range of poxviruses.

claim: A process involving the frequent appearance of DNA transposons in some insect viruses suggests an analogous mechanism for the spread of transposable elements between insect species.
source: A process involving the frequent appearance of DNA transposons in some insect viruses suggests an analogous mechanism for the spread of transposable elements between insect species (Gilbert et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Processed pseudogene products are enriched for highly expressed genes.
source: In cases of retrotransposition of host transcripts, the resulting processed pseudogene products are enriched for highly expressed genes (Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The overrepresentation of certain transcripts might provide clues for understanding and predicting how viruses might adapt with repurposed genes mimicking host functions.
source: The overrepresentation of certain transcripts might provide clues for understanding and predicting how viruses might adapt with repurposed genes mimicking host functions (Elde and Malik, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: Currently recognized cases of HGT involve oncogenes, regulators of translation like eIF2α, and antiviral genes that are highly expressed in response to infection.
source: Currently recognized cases of HGT involving oncogenes, regulators of translation, like eIF2α, and antiviral genes that are highly expressed in response to infection.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of known HGT cases.

claim: Repetitive TSDs generated by LINE-1 activity may enhance poxvirus adaptation by facilitating rapid gene copy number amplification of horizontally transferred genes on arrival.
source: Repetitive TSDs generated by LINE-1 activity may also enhance poxvirus adaptation by facilitating rapid gene copy number amplification of horizontally transferred genes on arrival.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed gene duplications and the presence of TSDs.

claim: Increases in gene copy number augment the probability of beneficial mutations appearing, allowing for swift diversification of newly acquired genes.
source: Increases in gene copy number augment the probability of beneficial mutations appearing, allowing for swift diversification of newly acquired genes (Elde et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The repetitive termini of poxvirus genomes enable the emergence and persistence of acquired genes predominately at the ends of the genome.
source: Thus, form follows function as the repetitive termini of poxvirus genomes further enable the emergence and persistence of acquired genes predominately at the ends of the genome (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the genomic features and observed patterns of gene distribution.

claim: As beneficial virus gene variants endure, they end up closer to the center of the genome as subsequently captured genes appear near the ends.
source: As beneficial virus gene variants endure, they end up closer to the center of the genome as subsequently captured genes appear near the ends.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed pattern of gene distribution in poxvirus genomes.

claim: Similar mechanisms of virus adaptation by HGT may be shared by other diverse classes of nucleocytoplasmic DNA viruses (NCLDVs), in addition to poxviruses.
source: Similar mechanisms of virus adaptation by HGT may be shared by other diverse classes of nucleocytoplasmic DNA viruses (NCLDVs), in addition to poxviruses (Deeg et al., 2018; Koonin and Yutin, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications, supported by citations.

claim: Many giant viruses encode a variety of genes acquired by HGT, including ribosomal genes.
source: Many giant viruses, which can exceed a megabase in genome size and infect diverse host species, encode a variety of genes acquired by HGT, including ribosomal genes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about giant viruses.

claim: Other classes of transposable elements may spur NCDLV evolution by mobilizing host genes into virus genomes across diverse ecosystems.
source: Given a primary role for LINE-1 elements in facilitating gene transfer, we speculate that other classes of transposable elements may spur NCDLV evolution by mobilizing host genes into virus genomes across diverse ecosystems.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.
